listenings.text: Let me explain our study in two ways. For specialists: we measure peripheral sensitization in patients with neuropathic pain. Now let me put it more simply. Peripheral sensitization refers to nerves that become too sensitive. Imagine a fire alarm which goes off when you only light a candle. That is what happens in these patients. A nerve that is damaged sends pain signals for very small things, like the touch of a shirt. In other words, the alarm is broken, not the house. So when I say sensitization, what I mean is a pain system that reacts too much. Our goal is to find a drug that calms the alarm without switching it off completely.

When I started teaching, I used a lot of jargon. I thought it made me sound like an expert. Then one day, a student who sat in the first row said: Professor, I understand every word, but not one sentence. That changed everything for me. Now I follow three rules. First, every technical word that I use gets a simple explanation, in the same sentence. Second, if I see a confused face, I do not repeat the same words louder. I paraphrase. I say the idea in a different way, often with an example from daily life. Third, I check. I ask: does that make sense? It takes ten more seconds, but people remember the idea, and not only the words.
